summary: The verb occurs once: Yahweh, silent for a long time, cries out like a woman in labour. Aramaic uses the root for an animal's cry, a lamb's bleat. The viper אֶפְעֶה shares the spelling, with a cognate in Arabic, but how it relates to the cry is not established.

words.summary: Its one use is Isa 42:14. BDB's count for it includes the three uses of the viper, which are spelled the same.

senses.definition: Cry out aloud, like a woman in labour; said by Yahweh of his breaking a long silence.

evidence.note: כַּיּוֹלֵדָה אֶפְעֶה, like a woman giving birth I will cry out, I will gasp and pant; set against I have kept silent, I have restrained myself.

opposites.note: I have kept quiet from of old... now I will cry out.

parallels.note: I will cry out, I will gasp and pant together.

words.summary: A venomous snake. Its Arabic cognate shows the older ʿ behind its ע. Whether it was named for the snake's hiss, from the root's cry, is not clear.

senses.definition: A venomous snake of the desert, whose bite kills.

evidence.note: He sucks the poison of cobras; the viper's tongue kills him.
In the land of trouble, with the lioness and lion, the viper and the flying serpent.
When an egg is crushed, a viper hatches.

cognates.note: A malignant kind of serpent; تفعّى, become like the viper in evil.
Of animals: the lambs bleated (Targum Sheni to Esther 1:2).

Segert's glossary gives pġt 'girl' (KTU 4.349:3, beside pġy 'boy') and a woman's name (KTU 1.19 II 6), the sister of Aqhat. If the midwife's name פּוּעָה goes with it, her ע stands for an older ġ, not the ʿ of the viper's Arabic. The scanned text's OCR garbles the ġ; the reading is from the glossary's order and its cross-reference to pġy.

note: Left out: פָּעוּ / פָּעִי Pau (q.cd.ac), the Edomite city, a place name awaiting its own entry. The midwife פּוּעָה is names/puah; BDB files her without a root (q.ap.ae). The Issacharite פּוּאָה / פֻּוָּה (q.am.ab) is spelled with א and is not filed here. uga-pgt is named only by names/puah. Leads not yet followed: Arabic فَاغِيَة, the flower of henna (Lane p. 2423, n34257), another ġ word; Ge'ez ʾafʿot and Ugaritic ảpʿ 'viper' (not in Segert's glossary); Syriac has no root פעא in SEDRA.
